en: Poor lord, listen to us—
If you would destroy us, here we stand!
If you send us, the road of the journey is here;
If you pour out your fury, lord, here we stand!"
The young lord was a tiger,
A saint born greater still
Than his father, gray-maned Manas.
He hung close around his neck
The gray purse left by Manas.
That poor lion, speaking timidly,
Appealed to his young men;
Showing that he was their lord,
He placed Kulchoro on his right,
And Kanchoro on his left,
He seated both upon his knees,
His mind filled with boundless thoughts,
And fondled the young men:
"My matched pair of lions,
While your heroic elder still has life,
For the two boys left among the khans
Like crows upon
A stake of black steel,
It is not merely my wife, young men—
My own dark life is yours in sacrifice!
Young men, leave my kinsman and take my household;
Leave the two of us and take the one;
Leave my wealth and take my encampment;
If you wish, take the wife you struck!"
Raging and distraught,
He pleaded with the two servants.
When he heard what had happened to the falcon,
He shouted, "Baabedin!"
And raised the battle cry, "Manas!"
Semetey rejoiced greatly,
As though his gray-maned father,
Tiger Manas, had returned to life.
He had a pale white mare caught
And sacrificed beneath the crescent hoof.
Semetey hurried with all his might,
Your hero, born more precious
Than Manas of the forty holy companions,
A hero who took after
His father, gray-maned Manas, without deviation.
The tent with golden cords
He had folded splendidly;
Striped felt and provisions
He had loaded upon Akborchuk.
He took a barren three-year-old horse for slaughter,
Rich fat for their provisions,
And red tea for their drink.
He had every piece of equipment packed,
And sour liquor and excellent food,
Saying, "Let the young men drink on the road,"
He loaded upon the packhorse.
The bulletproof Akolpok armor,
Armor fitted for Semetey,
He strapped behind
The companion who was Almambet's son.
The sight of it gladdened the heart.
With weapons and equipment upon his body,
That hesitant, poor fellow
Appeared as vast as Opol Mountain.
Driving the train behind him,
Because of his longing for Akshunkar,
And because of Aychurok's deed,
He drove fourteen horses from the Kyrgyz
At a pace beyond all measure.
The attendants he took as companions
Were all sons of khans.
The hesitant poor fellow's
Longing rested upon Churok.
His heart yearning and his breast aching,
That renowned hero, the great warrior,
With six grooms tending horses there,
And four men tending the cauldron,
Exactly twenty-five souls in all,
Set out, your hero, for Afghanistan
In pursuit of Aychurok.
The sight of him gladdened the heart:
Your gray-maned hero, taking after Manas,
His forefather and khan,
Looked altogether like Manas.
Of the champion chosen by Karan,
Which distinguishing mark shall we tell?
His brow was high, his wrath was strong;
The descendant of the tiger
Straightens all who challenge him.
He made that Buurul, seeming born of the unseen,
Step forward with a shimmering gait.
The sight opened every person's heart;
The poor man, lion-born,
Appeared surpassing in ancestral spirit,
Your gray-maned wolf, fraught with peril,
Would never turn back from an enemy.
His protectors numbered nine;
It was then they came to sustain
That poor man riding with a swagger.
His forty holy companions cried out
And gave their full protection
To the gray wolf of surpassing fortune.
Each possessed the awe of a thousand men;
The forty holy companions and Khydyr Ilyas
Surrounded the hero on every side.
Much of it is false and much is true;
No person has gone and seen it.
Half is invention and half is true;
Unless the Creator himself knows,
No person has returned from his presence.
The lions who departed long ago
We made into tales for our diversion,
So that we might relate the deeds
Of heroes who have vanished.
Your champion, son of the Bloodthirsty Manas,
Gladdened the heart that looked upon him.
He held the strength of a thousand men
And appeared like a gray hill.
He had the racehorse the Creator gave him,
His beast Buurul beneath him;
He had strength to slaughter alone
The swarming Chinese and Manchus.
Aquiline-nosed and stern of face,
Here was one worth an entire age.
If you observed the young lord, that gray wolf,
You could only marvel.
Ask nothing of the hero's nature:
He could throw an age into turmoil.
The pure Creator's name is great;
He creates every kind of living soul.
With fourteen swift horses in his train,
Having received an old saint's blessing,
Semetey rode eagerly,
Setting out toward Afghanistan.
His soul-companion Kulchoro
Resembled a glowing red ember.
The Creator makes souls of every kind;
No one like him seemed to exist in the world.
Slightly stooped and broad across the shoulders,
Of that gray wolf with a hero's frame,
Which quality shall we describe?
Kanchoro, the legacy left
By the gray-maned hero Chubak,
Was also broad across the right shoulder;
He was a hero who could rout the Oyrat.
His fortune stood complete,
And he too was a hero worth the world.
Yet he had one small flaw:
There was a black-hearted place within him.
Seized by restless ardor, they traveled on,
Covering a prodigious distance.
They raised toward the sky
The red banner left by Manas,
And heard reports from every side:
"Churok, daughter of Akun Khan,
Carried the falcon away
And took it with her," they heard.
They set their road toward Afghanistan,
Crossing ridge after ridge,
And land of rounded hills,
Fording winding streams,
And traversing curving mountains,
Passing rough and rolling sands,
And crossing countless lands.
When the sun sank dimly,
At beautiful Kary-Kyya
The hero turned aside to camp.
The poor lion, proud as a rooster,
Folded his arms behind his back;
Sighing as though weary,
Your gray wolf fell deep in thought,
He summoned his soul-companions,
And laid out the stones of the hearth;
Upon the stone hearth
He had the traveling cauldron boil.
He had the camp enclosed all around,
And a hitching post made of bronze
Planted firmly in the ground.
He spread out all their possessions,
Had Buurul stripped of his tack,
And tethered in the breeze.
He had deer-like Buurul
Roll splendidly in the sand,
Then had him tied apart
In fine fashion at that post.
The golden tent with silken cords
He had pitched in a breezy place
For his lord to sleep alone.
He had cushions of fine velvet
Laid thickly upon the ground.
No enemy could draw near
The gray wolf beset by peril:
At the hero's right hand
Lay a silver-cheeked battle-axe,
And at the hero's left side
Hung a gold-covered belt pouch.
The noble champion was worth the world,
His splendor unlike that of other men.
They kept the traveling cauldron boiling,
And spread all their goods around.
Your festive gray wolf
Had the tablecloth spread,
Had every delicacy brought,
And had a yearling lamb and young foal
Slaughtered with a slanting cut.
He had sugar heaped like snow,
And yellow butter piled in mounds.
They gnawed sugar white as snow,
And drank honey as though it were water;
They sliced kazy and ate the crest fat,
And ate bread dipped in honey.
My poor mother Kanykey,
A woman who understood honor,
Thinking, "He will need it on the road,"
Had employed all her wisdom:
Along the broad Talas
She had filly-mares tethered,
And strong liquor prepared.
Saying, "Let my son drink it on the road,"
From the honeyed kumis of those filly-mares
She had distilled this liquor.
With noise, delight, and revelry
They made exceeding merry,
And into the traveler's drinking bowls
They poured it to the brim.
They drank the liquor and grew merry,
Then slept propped upon their elbows,
Dozing briefly and resting,
Lying until their hips grew sore,
And reclining until sleep was satisfied.
They had the thoroughbreds brought in.
The cold dawn wind roared,
The tips of the grass swayed,
And the birds of morning chirped.
The earth seemed to split and open;
All the twilight mist
Scattered toward every quarter.
When one looked upon the face of the world,
It opened bright as a mirror.
Then gray wolf Semetey,
Telling tales for diversion,
That poor hero traveling the road,
Now raised his spyglass to look.
To a distance branching far away,
To a trackless place where horses had not gone,
Upon the pass of Agynek,
He rode his pacing horse for diversion,
Wishing to see the city of Afghanistan.
The tiger lord surged with eagerness;
That poor lion, never stirred before,
Young Semetey yearned
To catch sight of Churok,
As though he had gone mad.
Growing restless late in the day, the gray wolf
Took the great spyglass left by his father Manas
To cast his gaze across the face of the earth,
Of Aychurok, daughter of Akun,
And to obtain news from there.
